analysis.title: Unclear pause, but a clear tightening bias
key_insights: The FOMC held the target range at 3.75-4.0% on 28 Oct 2026, as expected. Two members dissented in favor of a 25bp hike: Hammack (expected) and Cook (unexpected).

The statement added a sentence: 'The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal.' JPMorgan reads it as a hawkish bias that keeps December live for the next hike.
JPMorgan continues to expect a rate hike at the December FOMC meeting.

The press conference did not clearly explain why the Committee held. Chair Warsh's answer mixed phrases such as 'new monetary medicine,' 'interrogating reality' and 'looking out the window.' JPMorgan says the market has become somewhat less convinced of a December hike as a result.
Warsh denied that the midterm elections influenced the decision. JPMorgan says a clearer explanation of the pause would have supported that denial.

Warsh said last month's hike is 'getting in the cracks,' meaning it is affecting broader financial conditions. JPMorgan notes Jeremy Stein coined the phrase with a different meaning, that rate changes are sometimes needed when macro-prudential policy falls short on financial stability risks.

The FOMC will keep eight meetings a year, but one meeting next year will focus on 'broad monetary policy strategy' instead of a policy decision. In 2028 two meetings will do so. Warsh gave no further details.

If the rest of the schedule is unchanged, there will be a 12- or 13-week gap between policy meetings for one or two meetings, which raises the importance of getting calibration right at those meetings.

JPMorgan questions the schedule change. Earlier framework reviews kept the policy meeting schedule intact, including during 2020, which showed the Committee can 'walk and chew gum.' Until the schedule is clarified, the market is left uncertain about the Committee's calendar.

Cook's dissent was a surprise. The September dot plot showed four participants favoring a hike in the last three meetings of the year, and most had assumed those were hawkish reserve bank presidents from the middle districts. Cook has not been seen as one of the more hawkish members.

The White House has tried for over a year to remove Cook as governor. The Supreme Court blocked that on procedural grounds, and the administration is pursuing another route, a hearing or tribunal at the White House in December. Asked whether he or the Fed would be involved, Warsh said 'not that I know of.'

macro_indicators.interpretation: The Committee held rates unchanged, as expected, with two dissents for a 25bp hike.
Cook's dissent was unexpected and signals a tightening bias reaching beyond the hawkish reserve bank presidents.
JPMorgan keeps its call for a hike in December. The market is somewhat less convinced after the press conference.

risk_factors: Unclear Fed communication on why the Committee paused, which has reduced market confidence in a December hike.
Uncertainty over the FOMC meeting schedule, including meetings focused on strategy and 12- to 13-week gaps between policy meetings.
Political pressure on the Fed, including the White House effort to remove Governor Cook and Warsh being asked about the midterms' influence.
geopolitical: The White House is pursuing a December hearing or tribunal on removing Fed Governor Cook, after the Supreme Court blocked the earlier removal attempt on procedural grounds.

tension_points.bull_case: JPMorgan reads the added statement sentence as a hawkish bias that keeps December live, and two dissents favored a hike now. It continues to expect a December hike.
tension_points.bear_case: The press conference gave no clear reason for the pause, and the market has become a little less convinced there is a plan to tighten in December. Williams and others have laid out arguments for a pause.
